cards.x: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) has a high propensity for going into the spinal fluid, so a lumbar puncture (spinal tap) is part of the work-up. Central nervous system involvement can occur, and it is an adverse risk factor, meaning it worsens the outlook. That is why the lumbar puncture is important.

cards.t: ALL treatment: Philadelphia-negative vs Philadelphia-positive
q: how is ALL treated
how does treatment differ if ALL is Philadelphia chromosome positive
when is stem cell transplant used in ALL
cards.x:
Treatment of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) depends on whether the leukemia carries the Philadelphia chromosome, t(9;22).

- Philadelphia-negative: pediatric-like regimens, usually for patients under 40: intensive chemotherapy in induction, consolidation and maintenance phases, with multiple chemotherapies, steroids and often targeted agents. Older adults may need therapy changes and adjustments to tolerate it.
- Philadelphia-positive: a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) plus chemotherapy.
- Allogeneic stem cell transplant where feasible, for adverse-risk or relapsed ALL.

cards.t: ALL prognosis and what patients are told
q: what is the prognosis of ALL
why is ALL survival better in children
what follow-up does an ALL patient need
cards.x:
The outlook in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is often positive, particularly for children: five-year overall survival under age 15 is about 90%, but it takes intensive chemotherapy for 2 to 5 years. For adults, five-year overall survival has historically been about 40%, with a cure rate that falls with age, though it is improving with new treatments, including immunotherapies.

Patients are referred to a hematologist/oncologist, ideally an ALL specialist. Most patients with acute leukemia are admitted to start work-up and treatment, then need frequent follow-up for labs and treatment, life-long surveillance, and consideration of clinical trials where feasible.

cards.t: Acute myeloid leukemia: what it is and who gets it
q: what is acute myeloid leukemia
who gets AML
how is AML different from ALL
cards.x:
Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a leukemia that starts in the myeloid progenitor or stem cells: very immature cells that can multiply rapidly. It occurs mostly in adults, particularly older adults over 60, and is unusual in children outside of neonates (newborns). Its signature finding is the Auer rod, which is pathognomonic (it points to this disease).

Quick way to tell it from acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL): ALL starts from lymphoid cells and has two age peaks, in children and around age 50, while AML starts from myeloid cells and is mainly a disease of older adults.

cards.t: Auer rods (pathognomonic for AML)
q: what are Auer rods
what does an Auer rod tell you
which leukemia has Auer rods
cards.x: Auer rods are thin, needle-shaped rods in the cytoplasm of a blast, and they are fused lysosomes. They are pathognomonic for acute myeloid leukemia (AML): seeing them on morphology (looking at the cells) confirms that the leukemia is myeloid. So a blast with an Auer rod points to a myeloid leukemia, not to acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL).

cards.t: AML risk groups and secondary AML
q: what is secondary AML
how is AML risk grouped
why does AML have so many subtypes
cards.x:
Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is not one uniform disease. It has multiple subtypes depending on the initial mutation and the stage of maturation, and a tremendous variety of cytogenetic abnormalities (chromosome changes) and mutations. Because of that, risk is broken down into favorable, intermediate and poor risk AML.

Secondary AML is AML that arises from another myeloid neoplasm, such as myelodysplastic syndrome or a myeloproliferative neoplasm, or after treatment of another cancer. It has poor outcomes.

cards.t: AML subtypes: the parts worth knowing
q: what are the subtypes of AML
which AML subtypes have extramedullary involvement
which AML subtype is APL
cards.x:
Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) subtypes were historically sorted into about 8 French-American-British (FAB) types and are now sorted into 18 subtypes recognized by the World Health Organization. Only a few points need real attention:

- Acute promyelocytic leukemia (M3) is its own topic, with its own treatment.
- Acute myelomonocytic leukemia (M4) and acute monocytic leukemia (M5) tend to have more extramedullary involvement, meaning disease outside the marrow.
- Acute erythroid leukemia (M6) and acute megakaryocytic leukemia (M7) are very rare.
- The first three types are undifferentiated AML, AML with minimal maturation and AML with maturation.

cards.t: Risk factors for AML
q: what are the risk factors for AML
how do AML and ALL risk factors differ
which age group is at risk for AML
cards.x:
Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) shares many risk factors with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), with a few differences. The virus link is HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) rather than Epstein-Barr virus, and the age group is adults over 60 rather than children under 5 and adults over 50.

- Radiation: prior high-dose radiation.
- Chemicals: benzene, petroleum and certain chemotherapies (alkylators).
- Viruses: HIV.
- Genetic syndromes: Down syndrome, Fanconi anemia and others; family history is a possible factor.
- Age and sex: adults over 60, and male gender.

cards.t: AML signs, symptoms and labs
q: what are the symptoms of AML
what white count is an emergency in AML
why do some AML patients have gum problems
cards.x:
Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) causes symptoms from too many immature white cells (blasts) and from immune dysfunction: anemia (fatigue, weakness, lightheadedness, shortness of breath, pale skin), thrombocytopenia (bruising, often petechiae or purpura, bleeding), infections, and B symptoms (weight loss, fever, night sweats). The myelomonocytic and monocytic subtypes may have gum involvement (hyperplasia, meaning overgrowth) or extramedullary disease.

Labs show anemia, thrombocytopenia and a white count that is often elevated but sometimes low (leukopenia). Unlike acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), a white count over 200K is rare, and any count over 100K needs emergent leukapheresis (a procedure that filters white cells out of the blood).

cards.t: How AML is diagnosed
q: how is AML diagnosed
how does flow cytometry tell AML from ALL
what blast percentage makes the diagnosis of AML
cards.x:
Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is confirmed with flow cytometry and bone marrow biopsy, the backbone tests. Flow cytometry identifies the leukemia's markers and separates AML from acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). The biopsy shows how much of the marrow is infiltrated and allows chromosome and mutation testing. Auer rods on morphology confirm myeloid origin. Also done: blood counts, electrolytes, coagulation, mutation sequencing and lumbar puncture.

The diagnosis means blasts of myeloid origin, historically 20% or more of the marrow; newer guidelines note that certain genetic mutations may allow the diagnosis with only 10% or higher, so references differ. Pancytopenia (low counts in all cell lines) can also come from infections, aplastic anemia, nutritional deficiencies and drugs, and flow cytometry separates these from AML because AML is clonal.

cards.t: AML treatment: fit vs unfit patients
q: how is AML treated
what is the 7 plus 3 regimen
who gets low-intensity therapy for AML
cards.x:
Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) treatment depends on how fit the patient is.

- Fit patients get intensive chemotherapy, often cytarabine plus an anthracycline (the regimen called 7 plus 3).
- Unfit patients get low-intensity therapy, frequently a hypomethylating agent, with or without venetoclax.
- Whatever the first treatment, allogeneic stem cell transplant is typically used for most intermediate- and high-risk patients, but only if they achieve remission.

cards.t: AML prognosis
q: what is the prognosis of AML
who does best and worst with AML
how many AML patients survive 5 years
cards.x:
Treatment brings an initial remission in many people with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), but it frequently relapses and treatment-related mortality is high. Overall survival is only 48% at 1 year and about 25 to 30% at 5 years. Aside from acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), survival is highest for favorable-risk AML (about two thirds alive at 5 years) and for younger patients. It is lowest for patients over 70 (only 5% alive at 5 years) and for adverse-risk or secondary AML (about 10% overall).

Patients are referred to a hematologist/oncologist, ideally a leukemia specialist, and most are admitted to start work-up and treatment. They need frequent follow-up, life-long surveillance and consideration of clinical trials.

cards.t: Acute promyelocytic leukemia: what it is and what causes it
q: what is acute promyelocytic leukemia
what chromosome change causes APL
why is APL different from other AML
cards.x:
Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) is a rare subtype of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) (M3 in the older French-American-British numbering). It is caused by arrested differentiation at the promyelocyte stage, meaning the cells get stuck at that stage instead of maturing.

The cause is a translocation (a swap of pieces) between chromosomes 15 and 17, written t(15;17), which fuses two genes called PML (the first) and RARA (the second). That PML-RARA fusion is the hallmark.

cards.t: APL presentation: bleeding, DIC and early mortality
q: how does APL present
why is APL an emergency
what is the prognosis of APL
cards.x:
Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) frequently presents with emergent complications, including bleeding and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), a clotting-system disorder (coagulopathy). Early mortality is high.

The key to remember is that if the patient survives the initial presentation, the prognosis is excellent, with a cure rate over 90%.

cards.t: APL treatment: ATRA plus arsenic trioxide
q: how is APL treated
does APL need chemotherapy
what is ATRA
cards.x:
Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) has a unique treatment: arsenic trioxide plus all-trans-retinoic acid (ATRA), a vitamin-type treatment. It is the one leukemia that does not need standard chemotherapy, which makes it the chemotherapy-free leukemia you can treat with a vitamin.

The work-up is the usual one for AML (flow cytometry, bone marrow biopsy, coagulation tests), and the t(15;17) translocation, the fusion of the two genes, marks the subtype.

cards.t: Myelodysplastic syndrome: what it is and how it develops
q: what is myelodysplastic syndrome
who gets MDS
why does MDS cause low blood counts
cards.x:
Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) are a group of myeloid malignancies defined by dysplasia, meaning myeloid cells that look abnormal. They often distort hematopoiesis and cause immune dysregulation and mutations. Clinically they show up as cytopenias, frequently anemia, with related fatigue, infections and bleeding.

MDS often evolves from milder abnormal stem cell clones (clonal hematopoiesis) until the dysplasia develops. The marrow is typically hypercellular (crowded), but the cells are not functional, which is why counts are low despite a full marrow. It is often idiopathic (no known cause) and seen in older people (median age 70), sometimes after prior chemotherapy or radiation, and it is more common in men.

cards.t: MDS vs AML: the 20% blast line
q: how do you tell MDS from AML
can MDS have blasts
what blast percentage makes it leukemia
cards.x:
The blast count is what separates myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) from leukemia. Higher-risk MDS can have blasts, but fewer than 20%. At 20% it is acute myeloid leukemia (AML). So 10% blasts is not leukemia, 15% is not leukemia, and 20% is.

The two overlap at the high end: very high-risk MDS has elevated blasts and substantial overlap with AML, and it carries a greater than 80% risk of AML within 5 years.

cards.t: MDS signs, symptoms and lab findings
q: how does MDS present
what lab findings are seen in MDS
why are many MDS patients found by accident
cards.x:
Many patients with myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) have no symptoms and are found incidentally. When symptoms come, they come from ineffective blood cell production and immune dysfunction: fatigue, weakness and pale skin from anemia, infections from ineffective white cells, and bleeding from a low platelet count.

Labs most frequently show anemia, plus neutropenia and occasionally thrombocytopenia. Neutrophils show abnormal morphology (shape), red cells are often abnormal (multinucleated or hyperplastic), and higher-risk MDS may have blasts but fewer than 20%.

cards.t: MDS treatment
q: how is MDS treated
what is the only cure for MDS
why be careful with growth factors in MDS
cards.x:
Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) treatment depends heavily on blood counts, risk status and mutations.

- Low risk with anemia: erythropoiesis-stimulating agents and red cell transfusions as needed.
- Neutropenia: myeloid growth factors, with care not to overstimulate the blasts.
- Higher risk: chemotherapy or hypomethylating agents.
- The only curative therapy is allogeneic stem cell transplant, but it is high risk and has a limited role.

cards.t: MDS prognosis by risk
q: what is the prognosis of MDS
how often does MDS turn into AML
what is the goal of treating low-risk MDS
cards.x:
Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) prognosis is highly variable and depends on risk. In lower-risk MDS, median survival is over 5 years and the risk of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is very low. In very high-risk MDS, median overall survival is 9 months and the risk of AML within 5 years is over 80%.

Low-risk patients often have complications from anemia, bleeding and/or infections, so the goal of treatment is quality of life.

cards.t: Myeloproliferative neoplasms: which cell line is overgrown
k: polycythemia vera vs essential thrombocythemia vs myelofibrosis
q: what are myeloproliferative neoplasms
how do the three myeloproliferative neoplasms differ
which cells are overproduced in each myeloproliferative neoplasm
cards.x:
Myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN) are rare myeloid malignancies in which mature cell lines proliferate abnormally. The easy way to tell them apart is by which cell line is overproduced:

- Polycythemia vera: red blood cells, which increases blood viscosity (thickness).
- Essential thrombocythemia: platelets.
- Myelofibrosis: mature myeloid cell lines (all of the myeloid lines), eventually causing fibrosis (scarring) of the marrow.
- Chronic myelogenous leukemia belongs to the same group and overgrows granulocytes.

cards.t: Polycythemia vera: too many red cells, JAK2 and itching after a warm bath
q: what is polycythemia vera
what mutation causes polycythemia vera
what is the classic symptom of polycythemia vera
cards.x:
Polycythemia vera is a myeloproliferative neoplasm in which the body over-produces red blood cells, which increases blood viscosity. It commonly results from a mutation in JAK2 (Janus kinase 2).

The presentation is usually nonspecific: fatigue, headaches and blurry vision. The classic clue is pruritus (itching) after warm baths or showers. Complications are thrombosis (clots), splenomegaly (an enlarged spleen) and bleeding.

cards.t: Polycythemia vera treatment and prognosis
q: how is polycythemia vera treated
what is the prognosis of polycythemia vera
how often does polycythemia vera turn into leukemia
cards.x:
Polycythemia vera is treated with phlebotomy (removing blood) and hydroxyurea. The prognosis is excellent, with an estimated survival of 14 years, and leukemic transformation (turning into leukemia) is rare, about 5% of cases.

Patients are referred to a hematologist and advised to stop smoking.

cards.t: Polycythemia vera vs essential thrombocythemia vs myelofibrosis
k: which MPN has the worst prognosis
q: what is the difference between polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia and myelofibrosis
which myeloproliferative neoplasm is the most aggressive
how do the myeloproliferative neoplasms differ in treatment and prognosis
cards.x:
All three myeloproliferative neoplasms involve mutations in the JAK (Janus kinase) and STAT (signal transducer and activator of transcription) signaling pathway, with JAK2 (Janus kinase 2) the named one in polycythemia vera. They differ in what is overproduced and how they behave.

- Polycythemia vera: too many red cells, so thicker blood. Classic clue is itching after a warm bath or shower. Treated with phlebotomy and hydroxyurea. Excellent prognosis, with estimated survival of 14 years.
- Essential thrombocythemia: too many platelets. Mostly no symptoms, but clotting or bleeding can happen. Treated with aspirin, hydroxyurea or other agents to reduce clotting risk. Generally a normal life span.
- Myelofibrosis: all myeloid lines overproduced, then scarring of the marrow, with a large spleen. Often treated with JAK inhibitors, which are palliative. It is the most aggressive of the three, and prognosis ranges from 10 to 15 years in low risk to often under 2 years in high risk.

cards.t: Myelofibrosis: marrow scarring and a big spleen
q: what is myelofibrosis
what causes myelofibrosis
how does myelofibrosis present
cards.x:
Myelofibrosis is a myeloproliferative neoplasm in which abnormal mutations in the JAK (Janus kinase) and STAT (signal transducer and activator of transcription) signaling pathway raise cytokine levels and cause a marked excess of all myeloid cell lines. Eventually this causes fibrosis (scarring) of the marrow.

The presentation is usually nonspecific: fatigue, and abdominal symptoms from splenomegaly (an enlarged spleen), meaning pain, early satiety (feeling full quickly) and bloating. Night sweats, fever and weight loss are also common. It is the most aggressive of the myeloproliferative neoplasms.

cards.t: Myelofibrosis complications, treatment and prognosis
q: what are the complications of myelofibrosis
how is myelofibrosis treated
what is the prognosis of myelofibrosis
cards.x:
Complications of myelofibrosis include severe splenomegaly, portal hypertension, bleeding, and progression to secondary acute myeloid leukemia. Treatment is often with targeted inhibitors of the Janus kinase pathway, called JAK (Janus kinase) inhibitors, which are palliative.

The prognosis is highly variable: low-risk patients can live 10 to 15 years, while high-risk patients often live less than 2 years. Patients are referred to a hematologist at diagnosis.

cards.t: Essential thrombocythemia: too many platelets
q: what is essential thrombocythemia
how is essential thrombocythemia treated
what is the prognosis of essential thrombocythemia
cards.x:
Essential thrombocythemia is a myeloproliferative neoplasm that over-produces platelets. It is often caused by gene mutations in the JAK (Janus kinase) and STAT (signal transducer and activator of transcription) signaling pathway and is rarely inherited.

Most patients have no symptoms, but some present with clotting (headaches, fatigue, paresthesias or vision changes) or with bleeding. Clotting can lead to a stroke or a heart attack. Treatment is aspirin, hydroxyurea or other agents to reduce clotting risk. The prognosis is excellent, with a generally normal life span with appropriate management, and patients are referred to a hematologist and advised to stop smoking.

cards.t: Why very high platelets can cause bleeding (acquired von Willebrand deficiency)
q: why does essential thrombocythemia cause bleeding
how can a high platelet count cause bleeding
cards.x: In essential thrombocythemia, bleeding can occur even though the platelet count is high. The reason is acquired von Willebrand factor deficiency: a shortage of von Willebrand factor at the site of injury. So a patient with this disease can be at risk of clotting (including a stroke or a heart attack) and of bleeding at the same time.

cards.t: Chronic myelogenous leukemia: what it is
q: what is chronic myelogenous leukemia
how did tyrosine kinase inhibitors change CML
how does CML progress
cards.x:
Chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) starts in hematopoietic stem cells but produces increased numbers of granulocytes, which are more mature than blasts. Its hallmark is a mutation that joins two genes, BCR (one gene) and ABL (another gene), through a fusion of chromosomes 22 and 9, which is the Philadelphia chromosome.

Historically it progresses from a chronic condition to acute leukemia in about 4 to 6 years. Until tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) arrived it was considered fatal; now it is largely a chronic disorder, and most patients have long-term survival and a good prognosis.

cards.t: The Philadelphia chromosome and the BCR-ABL fusion protein
q: what is the Philadelphia chromosome
how does BCR-ABL cause cancer
what does BCR-ABL do inside the cell
cards.x:
The Philadelphia chromosome comes from a translocation (a swap of pieces) between chromosomes 9 and 22. It attaches the gene called BCR (the first gene) to the gene called ABL (the second gene) and makes a fusion protein. That BCR-ABL protein is a functional enzyme that promotes cell proliferation and reduces apoptosis (programmed cell death), so the cell cannot turn off and constantly divides.

This is the hallmark of chronic myelogenous leukemia, and the same abnormality is the most common mutation in adult acute lymphoblastic leukemia.

cards.t: Who gets CML
q: who gets chronic myelogenous leukemia
what are the risk factors for CML
what share of leukemias is CML
cards.x: Chronic myelogenous leukemia makes up 15 to 20% of all leukemias. The median age at diagnosis is 45 to 55, and it affects either sex but is slightly more common in men. It may be more common in radiation bomb victims in Japan, but there are no other identified risk factors.

cards.t: CML signs, symptoms and labs
q: how does CML present
what is the white count in CML
why are many CML patients found by accident
cards.x:
About half of patients with chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) have no symptoms at diagnosis and are found from leukocytosis on a complete blood count. Others have anemia (fatigue, weakness, lightheadedness, shortness of breath), abdominal swelling or discomfort from splenomegaly, and B symptoms (weight loss, fever, night sweats, loss of appetite).

Labs show marked leukocytosis, thrombocytosis (a high platelet count) and anemia. The white count is often over 100K and can reach 500K, platelets are usually elevated, and blasts are usually very low unless the disease is in the accelerated or blast phase.

cards.t: How CML is diagnosed: PCR for BCR-ABL
q: how is CML diagnosed
what does PCR show in CML
how is CML response monitored
cards.x:
Chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) is confirmed by bone marrow biopsy and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing for the BCR (one gene) and ABL (another gene) fusion. A positive PCR for BCR-ABL in a patient with a marked increase in granulocytes confirms the diagnosis, and the same assay is also used to monitor response to treatment.

In the chronic phase, the marrow shows marked granulocytic proliferation and myelocytes. Flow cytometry (to check the cell lineage) and mutation analysis are also done.

cards.t: CML vs myelofibrosis and vs infection
q: how do you tell CML from myelofibrosis
how do you tell CML from an infection causing a high white count
cards.x:
Two things can be confused with chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML). The first is another myeloproliferative disorder, namely myelofibrosis. In CML the red cell morphology is normal and the hematocrit is not elevated, and the diagnosis is definitive when the fusion of the BCR (one gene) and ABL (another gene) is positive on polymerase chain reaction.

The second is reactive leukocytosis from some infections. There the spleen is not enlarged, the white count is usually under 50K, and BCR-ABL is not positive.

cards.t: The three phases of CML: chronic, accelerated and blast
q: what are the phases of CML
what is blast crisis in CML
how does accelerated phase differ from chronic phase
cards.x:
Chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) moves through three phases, marked mainly by how many blasts are present. Roughly 85 to 90% of patients present in the chronic phase, about 4 to 5% in the accelerated phase and about 1 to 2% in the blast phase.

- Chronic (stable) phase: no or few blasts (under 5%), an early proliferative phase with an excellent prognosis.
- Accelerated phase: often 10 to 19% blasts, possibly dysplastic changes in granulocytes and fibrosis, and frequently significant splenomegaly.
- Blast phase (blast crisis): behaves like an acute leukemia, usually acute myeloid leukemia (AML)-like, often with unique chromosomal and mutational abnormalities. It needs AML-like regimens and responds poorly to tyrosine kinase inhibitors.

cards.t: CML treatment: tyrosine kinase inhibitors
q: how is CML treated
what is the role of tyrosine kinase inhibitors
when is a transplant used in CML
cards.x:
Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) are the hallmark of therapy for chronic phase chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML), and there are 6 approved agents with different considerations. Advanced CML (accelerated or blast phase) has different considerations.

Allogeneic stem cell transplant is used in young healthy patients with resistance to TKIs or with advanced-stage CML.

cards.t: CML treatment milestones: BCR-ABL levels at 3, 6 and 12 months
q: what BCR-ABL level should a CML patient have at 3, 6 and 12 months
how is CML response monitored
what does a warning result mean in CML
cards.x:
The level of the BCR (one gene) and ABL (another gene) fusion is checked in the blood over time, and each checkpoint has a target. The optimal result is a BCR-ABL level under 10% at 3 months, under 1% at 6 months and under 0.1% at 12 months, so the level should keep falling by about a log step (a tenfold drop) at each milestone. After 18 months the ranges are the same as at 12 months, and under 0.01% is the treatment-free remission range.

Missing the target lands in a warning zone: over 10% at 3 months, 1 to 10% at 6 months, and 0.1 to 1% at 12 months (and after 18 months). The failure zone is over 10% at 6 months and over 1% at 12 months (and after 18 months); no failure level is listed at 3 months. A warning or failure result means a change of treatment.

cards.t: CML prognosis and stopping treatment
q: can CML patients stop their medication
what is the prognosis of CML
what is the outlook for accelerated or blast phase CML
cards.x:
Most patients with chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) now live normal lives while on tyrosine kinase inhibitors, and many live a full life with no detriment to long-term survival if appropriately managed. Treatment is for life unless the patient has kept a major molecular response (MMR) for 2 years, a sustained major molecular remission. Then stopping becomes possible. Recurrence after stopping happens in 50%, but most who recur can recapture deep responses.

Outcomes in accelerated or blast phase remain poor, with a median survival under 12 months, and those patients should be considered for clinical trials.

cards.t: Blood cancers across the lifespan: infants to the elderly
q: which blood cancers occur in each age group
how does care differ for children and older adults with leukemia
what age is acute myeloid leukemia most common
cards.x:
Each age group has its own pattern.

- Infants: acute myeloid leukemia is unusual in children outside of neonates.
- Children: acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is the most common malignancy under 15, with 5-year survival over 90%, peaking under age 5. Hyperdiploidy, mostly in children, is favorable, and Down syndrome and Fanconi anemia raise ALL and acute myeloid leukemia risk.
- Adolescents: the under-15 ALL figures are the closest group, and Philadelphia-negative ALL patients under 40 get pediatric-like regimens, which covers teenagers.
- Adults: ALL has a second peak around 50 with poor outcomes over 40 (about 30 to 40% long-term remission), and the fusion of BCR (one gene) and ABL (another gene) is the most common adult ALL mutation. Chronic myelogenous leukemia has a median age of 45 to 55.
- Elderly: fitness dictates prognosis. ALL needs therapy adjustments; acute myeloid leukemia is mostly over 60, with unfit patients getting low-intensity therapy and only 5% of those over 70 alive at 5 years; myelodysplastic syndrome has a median age of 70, and low-risk disease is treated for quality of life.

cards.t: Referral, admission and follow-up for blood cancers
q: who should manage a patient with leukemia
what follow-up do blood cancer patients need
when do patients with leukemia get admitted
cards.x:
Patients with blood cancers are managed by a hematologist/oncologist, and for the acute leukemias ideally a specialist. Most patients with acute leukemia are admitted for work-up and to start treatment. They then need frequent follow-up for labs and treatment, life-long surveillance, and consideration of clinical trials where feasible.

For the myeloproliferative neoplasms, the referral is to a hematologist, with advice to stop smoking in polycythemia vera and essential thrombocythemia. For chronic myelogenous leukemia, treatment is for life unless there has been sustained remission for 2 years.

cards.t: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and small lymphocytic lymphoma
q: what is chronic lymphocytic leukemia
is CLL the same as small lymphocytic lymphoma
what cells are involved in CLL
cards.x:
Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is a cancer of mature B cells, a type of lymphocyte (white blood cell). The cancerous cells build up in the blood, bone marrow, lymph nodes and spleen. It is clonal, meaning every cancer cell descends from one mutated B cell.

Small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL) is the same disease under a second name: when the cells are mostly in the blood it is called a leukemia, and when they are mostly in the lymph nodes it is called a lymphoma. Do not confuse it with the rare mature T-cell version, which is called T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia.

cards.t: The four chromosome changes behind CLL
q: what chromosome changes cause CLL
what is trisomy 12 in CLL
how common are the chromosome abnormalities in CLL
cards.x:
About 80% of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) cases come from loss or addition of chromosomal material in one of four chromosome changes: deletion 13q, deletion 11q, trisomy 12, or deletion 17p. A deletion means a piece of a chromosome is missing, and trisomy means there is an extra copy of chromosome 12.

The mutation arises in a mature B cell, which then multiplies as a single clone, so the cancer cells are all copies of that one mutated cell. Think of it as one photocopied mistake being reproduced over and over.

cards.t: Who gets CLL: age, sex, ancestry and risk factors
q: who gets chronic lymphocytic leukemia
what are the risk factors for CLL
how old are people when they are diagnosed with CLL
cards.x:
Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is a disease of older adults: the median age at diagnosis is 70. It is twice as common in males, and it is more common in people of Eastern European or Jewish descent. It accounts for 1% of all new cancer cases in the United States.

Age, male sex and that ancestry are the risk factors named. There are no known occupational or environmental risk factors, so workplace or chemical exposure is not part of the standard CLL picture (some other references do link certain exposures such as pesticides to CLL, so references differ).

cards.t: CLL signs and symptoms: painless nodes and a high white count
q: how does CLL present
why do people with CLL get infections or bruise easily
what is the classic finding in chronic lymphocytic leukemia
cards.x:
The classic picture of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is a high white blood cell count (lymphocytosis) together with painless lymphadenopathy, meaning enlarged lymph nodes that are firm and mobile, either in one area or widespread (50 to 90% of cases). The lymphocyte count must be above 5K (5,000) and is often above 100K. Many patients feel fine and the disease is found on routine blood work.

The other symptoms match what is failing in the blood: anemia causes fatigue, a low platelet count (thrombocytopenia) causes easy bruising and bleeding, and ineffective white cells lead to infections. About 40% have an enlarged spleen, less often an enlarged liver, and 5 to 10% have B symptoms (weight loss, night sweats, fevers).

cards.t: How CLL is diagnosed: flow cytometry, CD19 and CD5
q: how do you diagnose CLL
why is a bone marrow biopsy not needed for CLL
what does flow cytometry show in CLL
cards.x:
Flow cytometry is the test that confirms chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL). It reads the markers on the blood lymphocytes and shows whether they are one clonal population of B cells. CLL cells carry two cell-surface markers together, CD19 (cluster of differentiation 19) and CD5 (cluster of differentiation 5), and that pairing is the classic hallmark, called pathognomonic (specific enough to point to the disease by itself). That is why a bone marrow biopsy is usually not needed.

The count criterion is an absolute lymphocyte count above 5K (5,000) for 3 months, or below 5K when there are enlarged nodes or other symptoms. Cytogenetics (looking at the chromosome changes) are also done because they matter for prognosis and have some treatment considerations.

cards.t: Monoclonal B lymphocytosis and other look-alikes of CLL
q: what is monoclonal B lymphocytosis
how is monoclonal B lymphocytosis different from CLL
what else can look like CLL
cards.x:
Monoclonal B lymphocytosis is a raised lymphocyte count that stays under 5K (5,000), with no enlarged nodes, no enlarged organs, no low blood counts and no symptoms. It is not yet chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), but it progresses to CLL at 1 to 2% per year. Quick way to tell them apart: a count under 5K still counts as CLL if the patient has enlarged nodes or other symptoms, whereas monoclonal B lymphocytosis has none of those.

Other things that can mimic CLL are atypical lymphocytosis with some infections, including pertussis, and other lymphoproliferative disorders such as Waldenström macroglobulinemia, hairy cell leukemia and lymphomas in a leukemic phase. These are told apart by the cells' shape (morphology) and their marker pattern (immunophenotype).

cards.t: Rai staging of CLL (stages 0 to IV)
q: how is CLL staged
what is Rai stage III
what is the difference between Rai stage I and II
cards.x:
Rai staging sorts chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) into stages 0 to IV using only the physical exam and blood tests, so no advanced imaging is needed. It describes prognostic groups and can help decide when to treat, since treatment starts with symptomatic disease or rapid progression. Each stage adds one finding to the lymphocytosis:
- Stage 0: lymphocytosis alone, no symptoms
- Stage I: plus enlarged lymph nodes
- Stage II: plus an enlarged liver and/or spleen (organomegaly)
- Stage III: lymphocytosis with anemia, with or without nodes or organomegaly
- Stage IV: lymphocytosis with low platelets (thrombocytopenia), with or without nodes, organomegaly or anemia

Anemia makes it stage III and low platelets make it stage IV, whatever the nodes and organs show. More contemporary prognosis uses the CLL International Prognostic Index.

cards.t: Watch and wait: when CLL is not treated yet
q: when do you treat CLL
do all CLL patients need treatment right away
what is watch and wait
cards.x:
Many people with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) are not treated at first. Patients without symptoms are observed, called watch and wait, until there is evidence of rapid progression or disease-related symptoms. Rapid progression is defined as the lymphocyte count doubling in under 6 months.

The reasoning is that an isolated high white count alone does not equal treatment. A count that doubles within six months, or symptoms, is the trigger to treat. Care is managed by a hematologist/oncologist, and hospitalization is unlikely.

cards.t: CLL treatment: BTK inhibitors, venetoclax and antibodies
q: what drugs treat CLL
what is a BTK inhibitor
how is venetoclax used in CLL
cards.x:
Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is now treated mostly with targeted drugs, which have improved survival a great deal compared with older chemotherapy. There are three groups:
- Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitors: ibrutinib, acalabrutinib, zanubrutinib. Usually continuous if used alone.
- B-cell lymphoma 2 (BCL-2) inhibitors: venetoclax, combined with a monoclonal antibody for a fixed duration.
- Monoclonal antibodies: rituximab, obinutuzumab, ofatumumab.

For the patient this means a choice: a pill once or twice a day, indefinitely, or an infusion plus a pill that is time-limited but more intensive. The choice is likely based on patient preferences and mutations, and combination therapies are a growing trend.

cards.t: Richter transformation
q: what is Richter transformation
what happens when CLL transforms
why is Richter transformation important
cards.x:
Richter transformation is when chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) changes into an aggressive B-cell lymphoma. The outcomes are poor.

It matters because it is the exception to an otherwise good outlook. Most patients do well with CLL, with a five-year relative survival of about 88%, so the one development to watch for is the disease changing character into a fast, aggressive lymphoma.

cards.t: CLL prognosis and long-term outlook
k: die with CLL rather than from it
q: what is the prognosis of CLL
what is the survival rate for chronic lymphocytic leukemia
why do many CLL patients die with it rather than from it
cards.x:
The five-year relative survival for chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is about 88% (beginning in 2013), much improved over historical chemotherapy because of novel agents. More therapies are in development, including chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy and bispecific antibodies.

Because the disease starts at an advanced age and treatments keep improving, many patients will die with CLL rather than from it. A very good long-term prognosis is likely, follow-up is for lab monitoring and treatment, and the main long-term risk to know is Richter transformation, the change into an aggressive B-cell lymphoma.

cards.t: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma: the group, aggressive versus indolent
q: what is non-Hodgkin lymphoma
what is the difference between indolent and aggressive lymphoma
which lymphomas are aggressive and which are indolent
cards.x:
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) is a diverse group of cancers of lymphoid tissue that arise from B cells, T cells or natural killer (NK) cells and frequently present with enlarged lymph nodes. It is 4% of all new cancer diagnoses in the United States; 85% are B-cell and 15% are T-cell or NK-cell.

The key idea is the range from very aggressive to indolent (slow-moving):
- Very aggressive: Burkitt, diffuse large B-cell, T-cell leukemia/lymphoma
- Indolent: follicular, marginal zone, chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma
So the group runs from fast, fierce disease at one end to slow-moving disease at the other.

cards.t: Follicular lymphoma
q: what is follicular lymphoma
what causes follicular lymphoma
how is follicular lymphoma treated
cards.x:
Follicular lymphoma is the most common indolent histology of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. It typically shows up as painless lymphadenopathy that waxes and wanes. It is caused by the translocation t(14;18), which places the B-cell lymphoma 2 (BCL-2) gene on chromosome 14 and prevents cell death, so the cells survive when they should die. Under the microscope there are often clusters of packed follicles.

Frequently no treatment is needed (watch and wait). If symptomatic it may get intermittent low-intensity therapy, while high-risk disease may need more aggressive chemotherapy and immunotherapy. Rituximab is the drug named for low-grade B-cell lymphomas when treatment is required. It is incurable, but survival is often 10 to 15+ years, and indolent lymphomas can progress to an aggressive, difficult-to-treat lymphoma.

cards.t: Marginal zone lymphoma and MALT lymphoma
q: what is marginal zone lymphoma
what infection is linked to gastric MALT lymphoma
what is the link between hepatitis C and lymphoma
cards.x:
Marginal zone lymphomas are indolent non-Hodgkin lymphomas, making up 5 to 17% of all non-Hodgkin lymphoma and more common in older adults. There are three subtypes:
- Extranodal, or mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma: the most common subtype, in organs with mucosa such as the gastrointestinal tract, eyes and lungs. Two-thirds of gastric MALT cases are associated with H. pylori (Helicobacter pylori).
- Nodal marginal zone.
- Splenic marginal zone: associated with hepatitis C.

The memory hook is the infection link: stomach MALT goes with H. pylori, spleen goes with hepatitis C. If treatment is required for these low-grade B-cell lymphomas, it is rituximab.

cards.t: Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma (Waldenström macroglobulinemia)
q: what is Waldenström macroglobulinemia
why does Waldenström cause hyperviscosity
what mutation is seen in lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma
cards.x:
Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma is the same thing as Waldenström macroglobulinemia. It is an indolent lymphoma of lymphoplasmacytoid cells and plasma cells (terminally differentiated B cells), and a gene mutation (MYD88) is frequently found, in about 90% of cases.

The cells overproduce IgM, a large antibody. So much IgM thickens the blood (hyperviscosity), which often causes blurred vision and headache and, rarely, a stroke. Prognosis is good overall, with a relative five-year survival of 78%. Risk factors are genetic (familial) and environmental (farming, pesticides).

cards.t: Which gene change goes with which lymphoma
q: what translocation is in follicular lymphoma
what gene marks mantle cell lymphoma
which genetic marker goes with Burkitt lymphoma
cards.x:
Each lymphoma has a signature genetic change, and naming the change usually names the disease:
- t(14;18) with the B-cell lymphoma 2 (BCL-2) gene: follicular lymphoma. BCL-2 lands on chromosome 14 and prevents cell death.
- A gene mutation (MYD88) in about 90%: lymphoplasmacytic (Waldenström) lymphoma, with excess IgM and hyperviscosity.
- Cyclin D1 (a gene) with t(11;14): mantle cell lymphoma.
- MYC (a gene) upregulation: Burkitt lymphoma, which stimulates cell growth and division.
- Deletion 13q, deletion 11q, trisomy 12 or deletion 17p: chronic lymphocytic leukemia (80% of cases).

Infections link to two marginal zone types: H. pylori with gastric MALT (two-thirds of cases) and hepatitis C with splenic marginal zone.

cards.t: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL)
k: most common non-Hodgkin lymphoma in adults
q: what is diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
how does DLBCL present
can diffuse large B-cell lymphoma be cured
cards.x:
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is the most common non-Hodgkin lymphoma in adults, and it is aggressive. It is really a family with many subtypes and varieties, divided by location, mutations and infectious associations.

The typical story is a fast-growing mass or swelling, sometimes with B symptoms (fever, fatigue, night sweats, weight loss). Risk factors are older age, family history, autoimmune conditions, infections and environmental exposures. Treatment is multi-drug chemotherapy such as R-CHOP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin, prednisone). It is often treatable and curable with multi-agent chemotherapy; no single cure percentage is worth memorizing. Tumor lysis syndrome is a risk when treatment starts.

cards.t: Mantle cell lymphoma
q: what is mantle cell lymphoma
what translocation is in mantle cell lymphoma
who gets mantle cell lymphoma
cards.x:
Mantle cell lymphoma is a rare subtype of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, 5% of cases, identified by a translocation, t(11;14), that involves cyclin D1 (a gene). It typically has an aggressive course, although an indolent variant has been described, and that difference is why survival varies so widely: median survival ranges from under 2 years to over 9, depending on the variant.

It is more common in men, with a median age of 60 to 70 years. Its treatment is not covered separately; aggressive B-cell lymphomas in general get multi-drug chemotherapy.

cards.t: T-cell lymphomas and their subtypes
q: what are the types of T-cell lymphoma
what virus causes adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma
what is the most common T-cell lymphoma
cards.x:
T-cell lymphomas are a diverse group of non-Hodgkin lymphomas with many subtypes. The main ones to know:
- Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified: the most common T-cell lymphoma, one-third of cases.
- Anaplastic large cell lymphoma: aggressive.
- Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma: very aggressive and associated with human T-lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1), more common in the Caribbean, Central and South America.
- Extranodal natural killer (NK)/T-cell lymphoma: often affects the nasal region.
- Also listed: nodal, intestinal and hepatosplenic T-cell lymphomas.

As a group, T-cell lymphomas respond less well to treatment than B-cell lymphomas.

cards.t: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma: mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome
q: what is mycosis fungoides
what is Sézary syndrome
why does mycosis fungoides look like a fungal infection
cards.x:
Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma is a T-cell lymphoma that shows up in the skin. The form called mycosis fungoides presents with skin lesions that resemble fungal infections (despite the name, it is a lymphoma), which progress to nodular lesions that may ulcerate.

A more aggressive form is Sézary syndrome: a widespread red, itchy rash (erythroderma) that can cause severe pruritus and diminished quality of life. Treatment focuses on the skin, and there is often no visceral involvement, meaning the internal organs are not affected.

cards.t: Risk factors for non-Hodgkin lymphoma
k: lymphoma and HIV EBV HTLV-1 H pylori
q: what are the risk factors for non-Hodgkin lymphoma
which infections are linked to lymphoma
does immunosuppression raise lymphoma risk
cards.x:
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma risk factors fall into a few groups, and the infections are the ones to know best: HIV, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), human T-lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1) and H. pylori. The full list also includes hepatitis C, Lyme disease and human herpesvirus 8.
- Immunosuppression: prior immunotherapy, chemotherapy, radiation or malignancy, and prior transplantation.
- Autoimmune conditions (systemic lupus erythematosus, Sjögren, celiac) and Crohn disease.
- Environmental exposures, including DDT (farming).
- Higher incidence in White individuals, in developed countries and in males, plus family history.

cards.t: How non-Hodgkin lymphoma presents
q: what are the symptoms of non-Hodgkin lymphoma
what is extranodal lymphoma
how does primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma present
cards.x:
The main sign of non-Hodgkin lymphoma is peripheral lymphadenopathy (enlarged lymph nodes), present in more than two-thirds of patients. Other features are B symptoms (weight loss, night sweats, fever of unknown origin), rash, hypersensitivity reactions, fatigue, pruritus, malaise, ascites (fluid in the abdomen) and effusions.

About half develop extranodal disease, meaning lymphoma outside the lymph nodes. Central nervous system lymphoma causes headaches, lethargy and neurologic defects that mirror primary central nervous system cancers. Primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma causes a large mass in the mediastinum (the middle of the chest) with cough and an abnormal chest X-ray.

cards.t: Diagnosing lymphoma: excisional biopsy, never fine needle aspiration
q: how is non-Hodgkin lymphoma diagnosed
why not use fine needle aspiration for lymphoma
which lymphomas need a lumbar puncture
cards.x:
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is diagnosed by excisional lymph node biopsy, which removes the node so the pathologist can see its architecture. It is reserved for a node that is significantly enlarged (2 cm), persistent and progressively growing. Fine needle aspiration is avoided because it cannot show the node's architecture and may miss the diagnosis, so a negative one should not be trusted.

The rest of the work-up: imaging (usually computed tomography (CT) or positron emission tomography (PET)) to characterize and stage; a complete blood count (cytopenias suggest bone marrow involvement); chemistries (to rule out tumor lysis syndrome); lactate dehydrogenase (LDH); and a bone marrow biopsy. High-grade lymphomas, including Burkitt, also need a lumbar puncture.

cards.t: Lugano staging of lymphoma (the diaphragm rule)
k: staging above and below the diaphragm
q: how is lymphoma staged
what is the difference between stage 2 and stage 3 lymphoma
what does the diaphragm have to do with lymphoma staging
cards.x:
Lymphoma is staged by the Lugano classification, a modified version of the older Ann Arbor system, and everything depends on the diaphragm (the muscle separating chest from abdomen). It is used for non-Hodgkin and Hodgkin lymphoma alike.
- Stage 1: localized disease, a single lymph node region or a single organ
- Stage 2: two or more lymph node regions on the same side of the diaphragm
- Stage 3: lymph node regions both above and below the diaphragm
- Stage 4: widespread disease, multiple organs with or without lymph node involvement

Quick way to remember: one region is stage 1, two or more on one side is 2, both sides is 3, and organs are 4.

cards.t: Poor prognostic factors in non-Hodgkin lymphoma
q: what predicts a poor prognosis in non-Hodgkin lymphoma
does high LDH mean worse lymphoma prognosis
what is performance status in lymphoma
cards.x:
Five features predict a worse prognosis in non-Hodgkin lymphoma: age over 60, extranodal sites, a poor performance status (above 2 on the Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group scale, a rating of how well the patient can carry out daily activities), stage III or IV disease, and an elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH).

Two of these come straight from the work-up: stage from imaging and LDH from a blood test.

cards.t: Why LDH is checked in every lymphoma
q: why do you order LDH in lymphoma
what does a high LDH mean in lymphoma
cards.x:
Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is a blood test that is part of the work-up in anyone with a lymphoma. It is ordered as a marker of rapid proliferation, meaning how quickly the cancer cells are dividing and turning over. In non-Hodgkin lymphoma an elevated LDH is also one of the poor prognostic factors, alongside age over 60, extranodal sites, poor performance status and stage III or IV.

It sits with the blood count and chemistries: the blood count looks for low cell counts when the bone marrow is involved, the chemistries look for electrolyte problems that could signal tumor lysis syndrome, and LDH reflects how active the tumor is.

cards.t: Lymphoma treatment by type (rituximab, R-CHOP, CHOP without rituximab)
k: why no rituximab in T-cell lymphoma
q: how is non-Hodgkin lymphoma treated
what is R-CHOP
why is rituximab not used for T-cell lymphomas
cards.x:
Treatment of non-Hodgkin lymphoma depends on the type:
- A single node with non-aggressive disease: radiation.
- Low-grade B-cell lymphomas: rituximab (a monoclonal antibody) if treatment is required, with chemotherapy added if the disease is extensive.
- Aggressive B-cell lymphomas: often multi-drug chemotherapy, for example R-CHOP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin, prednisone). Some cancers get even more aggressive regimens.
- T-cell lymphomas: similar regimens minus rituximab.

The reason for dropping rituximab is that it targets CD20 (a protein on the cell surface), and T cells do not express CD20, so there is nothing for the antibody to bind.

cards.t: Tumor lysis syndrome
q: what is tumor lysis syndrome
why does tumor lysis syndrome cause kidney failure
what is the most dangerous part of tumor lysis syndrome
cards.x:
Tumor lysis syndrome is a medical emergency, an oncologic emergency, that happens when a tumor breaks down rapidly and releases its cell contents into the blood: potassium, phosphorus and uric acid. All three flood out at once.

It can cause acute renal failure, because uric acid and calcium phosphate crystals precipitate in the kidney tubules, which makes the problem worse. The largest risk, though, is high potassium (hyperkalemia), which can cause an arrhythmia and potentially death.

It is seen in aggressive lymphoma, can happen spontaneously in highly aggressive lymphomas such as Burkitt, and is also seen outside lymphoma, in acute lymphoblastic leukemia and acute myeloid leukemia with marked leukocytosis (very high white counts).

cards.t: Preventing tumor lysis syndrome: allopurinol and fluids
q: how do you prevent tumor lysis syndrome
what is allopurinol used for in lymphoma
what is the treatment for tumor lysis syndrome
cards.x:
Tumor lysis syndrome is anticipated rather than waited for. In aggressive lymphoma, allopurinol (a hypouricemic agent, meaning it lowers uric acid) and fluids are given in advance, before chemotherapy starts. Once it occurs, it requires aggressive intravenous (IV) fluid hydration.

The chemistries in the lymphoma work-up (the electrolytes) are checked to rule it out. For the patient, the instruction when starting treatment is simple: drink plenty of fluids and take allopurinol.

cards.t: Lymphoma prognosis: indolent versus aggressive, B-cell versus T-cell
k: T cells always worse than B cells
q: what is the prognosis of lymphoma
can indolent lymphoma be cured
are aggressive lymphomas curable
cards.x:
The two ends of the lymphoma range behave in opposite ways. Indolent lymphomas are incurable, but survival is often 10 to 15+ years with intermittent treatment, and they carry a risk of progressing to an aggressive, difficult-to-treat lymphoma. Aggressive lymphomas are the reverse: they are often treatable and often cured with chemotherapy, with five-year survival approximately 60 to 70%. Do not learn a single cure percentage for them.

T-cell lymphomas respond less well than B-cell lymphomas. In practice, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is often treatable and curable, while follicular lymphoma often needs no treatment or only intermittent treatment but cannot be cured.

cards.t: Lymphoma treatment complications and patient education
q: what are the complications of lymphoma chemotherapy
do lymphoma patients need to be hospitalized
who manages lymphoma care
cards.x:
Chemotherapy complications in lymphoma are infections, bleeding, anemia, electrolyte abnormalities and diarrhea, and they go with all chemotherapy agents.

Patients are referred to and managed by a hematologist, ideally a lymphoma expert. Aggressive lymphomas with electrolyte abnormalities may need hospitalization; otherwise treatment is often outpatient. Burkitt lymphoma also requires rapid transfer of care. When treatment starts, the instruction is to drink plenty of fluids and take allopurinol, which is aimed at preventing tumor lysis syndrome.

cards.t: Burkitt lymphoma: what it is and how it presents
q: what is Burkitt lymphoma
how does Burkitt lymphoma present
what gene is involved in Burkitt lymphoma
cards.x:
Burkitt lymphoma is a very aggressive B-cell lymphoma associated with upregulation of MYC (a gene), which stimulates cell growth and division. The result is a very rapidly growing, often painless swelling, so fast that changes can be visible over the course of a single day. One picture of it is a child with a huge, rapidly growing jaw swelling. B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss) are common.

The doubling time is extremely fast: the tumor may be seen expanding within the same 24 hours. That speed fits with how urgently it is managed and with tumor lysis syndrome, which can occur spontaneously, even before treatment.

cards.t: Burkitt lymphoma: endemic, sporadic and immunodeficiency-associated
q: what are the types of Burkitt lymphoma
which Burkitt type is linked to Epstein-Barr virus
who gets sporadic Burkitt lymphoma
cards.x:
Burkitt lymphoma comes in three types, separated by where and in whom it occurs:
- Endemic: largely sub-Saharan Africa and New Guinea, strongly associated with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV).
- Sporadic: typically the United States and Western Europe, more common in males, almost always under age 35.
- Immunodeficiency-associated: associated with HIV/AIDS.

Quick way to match them: the African and New Guinea, Epstein-Barr virus one is the endemic type; the one in the United States and Western Europe, mostly males under 35, is sporadic; the one linked to HIV is the immunodeficiency type.

cards.t: The starry sky pattern of Burkitt lymphoma
q: what is the starry sky appearance
what does starry sky mean on pathology
what lymphoma has a starry sky pattern
cards.x:
Starry sky is the classic pathology appearance of Burkitt lymphoma. Under the microscope there are sheets of dark lymphoma cells, which make up the sky, scattered with pale benign macrophages, which are the stars. The macrophages are clearing out the dying lymphoma cells.

So if a pathologist describes a starry sky, think Burkitt lymphoma.

cards.t: Burkitt lymphoma management and prognosis
q: how is Burkitt lymphoma treated
what is the prognosis of Burkitt lymphoma
why does Burkitt lymphoma need urgent treatment
cards.x:
Burkitt lymphoma needs treatment to start promptly, with an emergent referral to a hematologist and rapid transfer of care. Treatment is multi-agent chemotherapy, started with caution because of tumor lysis syndrome, so allopurinol and fluids are used. As a high-grade lymphoma, the work-up also includes a lumbar puncture.

Despite how fast it grows, the long-term prognosis is excellent if it is identified early and treated with multi-agent chemotherapy: the figures are more than 90% in children and 50 to 90% in adults.

cards.t: Hodgkin lymphoma and the Reed-Sternberg cell
q: what is Hodgkin lymphoma
what is a Reed-Sternberg cell
how does Hodgkin lymphoma spread
cards.x:
Hodgkin lymphoma is a B-cell lymphoma with an unusual makeup: only a few malignant cells, called Reed-Sternberg cells, sitting among a large number of normal immune effector cells. A Reed-Sternberg cell is a large, binucleated (two-nucleus) neoplastic B cell. When you see Reed-Sternberg cells, think Hodgkin lymphoma.

It makes up about 10 to 15% of all lymphoma diagnoses worldwide, and it is marked by contiguous spread, meaning it moves through the lymph nodes in an orderly fashion, one neighboring node group after another.

cards.t: Hodgkin lymphoma risk factors: two age peaks, siblings, Epstein-Barr virus
q: what are the risk factors for Hodgkin lymphoma
why is Hodgkin lymphoma bimodal
is Hodgkin lymphoma linked to Epstein-Barr virus
cards.x:
Hodgkin lymphoma has a bimodal incidence, meaning two age peaks: adults in their 20s and adults over 60. Same-sex siblings have a 10 times increased risk. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is suspected and is identified in 40 to 50% of cases. Others include HIV, human herpesvirus 6 and tuberculosis.

Bimodal simply means two separate age peaks, with a dip in between.

cards.t: How Hodgkin lymphoma presents: painless neck nodes, itching, alcohol pain
q: what are the symptoms of Hodgkin lymphoma
what is the alcohol pain sign in Hodgkin lymphoma
where does Hodgkin lymphoma usually show up
cards.x:
The usual presentation of Hodgkin lymphoma is painless, asymptomatic lymphadenopathy (70%), most often in the neck (cervical), though it can be supraclavicular (above the collarbone) or in the chest (mediastinal), where a mediastinal mass can be seen on chest X-ray.

Two clues stand out: pain in the nodes may worsen with alcohol consumption, and pruritus (itching) may be very intense if present. The spleen is enlarged in about 30% of patients, and the liver is sometimes enlarged.

cards.t: Hodgkin versus non-Hodgkin lymphoma
q: what is the difference between Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma
how do I tell Hodgkin from non-Hodgkin lymphoma
which lymphoma has Reed-Sternberg cells
cards.x:
Both are cancers of lymphoid tissue that usually show up as enlarged lymph nodes, but they are different groups.

- Hodgkin lymphoma: a B-cell lymphoma with a few malignant Reed-Sternberg cells (large, binucleated cells) among many normal immune cells; it spreads in an orderly way through neighboring lymph nodes; it has two age peaks, in the 20s and over 60; it is about 10 to 15% of lymphomas; it is treated with multi-drug chemotherapy by stage and is generally curable.
- Non-Hodgkin lymphoma: a diverse group from B cells (85%), T cells or natural killer cells, running from very aggressive to indolent; about half develop disease outside the lymph nodes; treatment depends on the type, such as multi-drug chemotherapy for aggressive B-cell lymphomas.

Both are diagnosed by excisional lymph node biopsy, never fine needle aspiration, and both are staged with the Lugano classification. Quick tell: Reed-Sternberg cells mean Hodgkin.

cards.t: Diagnosing Hodgkin lymphoma: excisional biopsy, CD15 and CD30
q: how is Hodgkin lymphoma diagnosed
what markers does classical Hodgkin lymphoma express
why avoid fine needle aspiration in Hodgkin lymphoma
cards.x:
Hodgkin lymphoma is diagnosed by excisional lymph node biopsy. Fine needle aspiration is avoided, because an excisional biopsy is needed to see the node's architecture and a needle sample may miss the diagnosis. Classical Hodgkin lymphoma expresses CD15 (a marker) and CD30 (another marker).

The rest of the work-up: a chest X-ray to look for a mediastinal mass or adenopathy, a complete blood count (cytopenias with marrow involvement), chemistries (to rule out tumor lysis syndrome), lactate dehydrogenase (rapid proliferation) and a bone marrow biopsy. Staging uses the Lugano classification, the same four stages as non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

cards.t: Hodgkin lymphoma treatment: ABVD and stage-based therapy
q: how is Hodgkin lymphoma treated
what is ABVD
why is bleomycin being replaced in Hodgkin treatment
cards.x:
Hodgkin treatment follows the stage, which guides the type of chemotherapy:
- Early stage I and stage II-A: a short course of chemotherapy (ABVD historically).
- Bulky stage I or II disease, or B symptoms: chemotherapy plus radiation.
- Stage III or IV: chemotherapy.

ABVD stands for Adriamycin (doxorubicin), bleomycin, vinblastine and dacarbazine. New novel agents are replacing bleomycin because of its pulmonary toxicities, meaning it can damage the lungs. A patient with painless lymphadenopathy who was treated with ABVD had Hodgkin lymphoma. (Many protocols also add radiation to short-course chemotherapy for early stages, so references differ.)

cards.t: Hodgkin lymphoma prognosis and delayed toxicities
q: what is the prognosis of Hodgkin lymphoma
what happens if Hodgkin lymphoma relapses
what are the late effects of Hodgkin treatment
cards.x:
Hodgkin lymphoma is generally curable, with more than 90% of patients alive at five years. If it relapses after first-line treatment, an allogeneic stem cell transplant (cells from a donor) may be required. (Many references describe salvage chemotherapy followed by an autologous transplant, using the patient's own cells, as the usual first step at relapse, so references differ.)

Results are inferior in older patients, with bulky disease, or with certain subtypes (lymphocyte depleted or mixed cellularity). Delayed toxicities may include myelodysplastic syndrome, secondary leukemia and other cancers.

cards.t: Plasma cell disorders: MGUS, smoldering myeloma and multiple myeloma
q: what are plasma cell disorders
how are MGUS, smoldering myeloma and multiple myeloma related
what is a plasma cell
cards.x:
Plasma cell disorders are a spectrum of malignant and premalignant conditions that arise from plasma cells, which are terminally differentiated B cells (the end of the B-cell line). The spectrum has three steps:
- Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS): no symptoms, fewer harmful plasma cells and proteins, a low risk of progression.
- Smoldering myeloma: no symptoms, but more plasma cells and protein.
- Multiple myeloma: symptoms throughout the body, and an incurable malignancy.

Multiple myeloma is 10% of all hematologic malignancies.

cards.t: How multiple myeloma causes its problems
q: why does multiple myeloma cause hypercalcemia
why does multiple myeloma damage the kidneys
what does a myeloma clone produce
cards.x:
Normal plasma cells make antibodies. In myeloma, clonal evolution produces one clone that overproduces a single type of antibody, most commonly IgG.

That sets off the main problems. The myeloma activates osteoclasts (cells that break down bone), releasing calcium into the bloodstream. Renal dysfunction often comes from light chain and calcium phosphate deposition in the kidneys. Anemia is multifactorial, from renal dysfunction and from bone marrow involvement.

cards.t: Risk factors for multiple myeloma
q: who gets multiple myeloma
what are the risk factors for myeloma
is myeloma more common in some races
cards.x: The risk factors for multiple myeloma are age, race, family history, a prior plasma cell disorder and exposures. Risk rises with age and most diagnoses are in people over 65. African Americans are at higher risk than other races. A prior monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) or smoldering myeloma raises risk, since those are the earlier steps of the same disease. Environmental exposures include radiation, chemical and occupational exposures.

cards.t: Multiple myeloma: the CRAB features
k: hypercalcemia renal insufficiency anemia bone lesions
q: what does CRAB stand for in myeloma
what are the symptoms of multiple myeloma
why do myeloma patients get infections
cards.x:
CRAB (hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions) is the set of features that make up the symptoms of multiple myeloma:
- C, calcium (hypercalcemia): constipation, increased thirst, urinary frequency, nausea.
- R, renal insufficiency: swelling.
- A, anemia: fatigue and shortness of breath.
- B, bone lesions and pain: often in the back, chest or pelvis.

Patients are also at higher risk of infections. The related picture adds amyloidosis, hyperviscosity and polyneuropathies.

cards.t: The SLiM markers in myeloma
q: what is SLiM in myeloma
what do the letters in SLiM stand for
can myeloma be asymptomatic
cards.x:
SLiM is the newer set of lab and imaging findings that go alongside CRAB (hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions), and it shows that myeloma may be asymptomatic yet still have these findings. The letters stand for:
- S: bone marrow plasma cells at 60% or more (plasmacytosis).
- Li: an abnormal light chain ratio, above 100 to 1.
- M: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showing 2 or more lesions.

So a myeloma-defining event is either a CRAB feature or one of the SLiM markers, even without symptoms.

cards.t: Punched out lytic bone lesions in myeloma
q: what are punched out lesions
what do myeloma bone lesions look like on X-ray
why does myeloma cause bone pain
cards.x:
Punched out lesions are the classic X-ray sign of multiple myeloma. On a skull radiograph they look like many small, round osteolytic holes, meaning bone has been dissolved away. They are the bone lesions of myeloma and the reason for bone pain, often in the back, chest or pelvis.

This fits the mechanism: myeloma activates osteoclasts, the cells that break down bone, so bone is destroyed and calcium enters the blood.

cards.t: Diagnosing multiple myeloma: 10% plasma cells plus a CRAB feature
k: myeloma vs acute leukemia blast percentage
q: how is multiple myeloma diagnosed
how many plasma cells are needed for myeloma
how is myeloma different from acute leukemia in the percent needed
cards.x:
Multiple myeloma is diagnosed when there are at least 10% plasma cells in the bone marrow (or a biopsy-proven plasmacytoma, a plasma cell tumor) plus one or more features of CRAB (hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions).

Contrast with acute leukemia: acute leukemia needs 20% blasts in the marrow, while myeloma needs only 10% plasma cells. The quieter relatives, monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance and smoldering myeloma, are asymptomatic.

cards.t: Monoclonal protein, SPEP and Bence Jones protein
q: what is Bence Jones protein
what does serum protein electrophoresis show in myeloma
what is an M protein
cards.x:
A monoclonal protein (M-protein) is the single overproduced antibody the myeloma clone makes. On serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP), a monoclonal protein is characteristic of myeloma.

A positive urine monoclonal protein is called Bence Jones protein. Worth remembering together: an anemic patient with bone pain, renal failure and Bence Jones protein has myeloma.

cards.t: Work-up for multiple myeloma
q: what tests do you order for multiple myeloma
how do you look for bone lesions in myeloma
what is beta-2 microglobulin used for
cards.x:
The work-up for multiple myeloma covers the blood, the urine, the marrow and the bones:
- Complete blood count and a metabolic/electrolyte panel.
- Serum protein electrophoresis and a 24-hour urine protein electrophoresis.
- Bone marrow biopsy with flow cytometry.
- Light chains (kappa and lambda), checking the ratio.
- Serum beta-2 microglobulin, which feeds into staging.
- Imaging for bone lesions, classically whole-body computed tomography (CT).

cards.t: Telling myeloma from MGUS, smoldering myeloma and other look-alikes
q: what else can look like multiple myeloma
how is Waldenström different from myeloma
what other conditions have a paraprotein
cards.x:
Multiple myeloma has to be told apart from several conditions that also produce an abnormal protein:
- Smoldering myeloma: a more indolent process, often monitored.
- Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS): asymptomatic.
- Waldenström macroglobulinemia: often makes an IgM monoclonal protein, with a different pathophysiology and treatment.
- Chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma, non-Hodgkin lymphoma and amyloidosis: others with a paraprotein.
- Reactive hypergammaglobulinemia: from conditions such as cirrhosis and chronic inflammation.

cards.t: R-ISS staging of multiple myeloma
q: how is multiple myeloma staged
what makes R-ISS stage III
does myeloma staging change treatment
cards.x:
R-ISS (Revised International Staging System) sorts myeloma into three prognostic groups using beta-2 microglobulin, albumin, chromosomal abnormalities and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). It is prognostic, but it does not broadly change treatment decisions.
- Stage I: beta-2 microglobulin below 3.5 mg/L, albumin 3.5 g/dL or higher, standard-risk chromosomes and a normal LDH.
- Stage II: anything that is not stage I or III.
- Stage III: beta-2 microglobulin of 5.5 mg/L or more regardless of albumin, high-risk chromosomal abnormalities (del 17p, t(4;14) or t(14;16)), and a high LDH (above the upper limit of normal).

Stage III is taught as requiring all of those together. The published system accepts either the high-risk chromosomes or the high LDH, so references differ.

cards.t: Multiple myeloma treatment: goals, drug backbone, transplant, relapse
q: how is multiple myeloma treated
is multiple myeloma curable
what is the goal of myeloma treatment
cards.x:
Myeloma is considered incurable, so the goal is to maintain prolonged remissions to improve survival and quality of life.

Newly diagnosed patients get a 3- or 4-drug regimen built on a proteasome inhibitor and an immunomodulatory drug (two drug classes), with steroids. If the patient is a transplant candidate, an autologous transplant (using the patient's own stem cells) improves overall survival, as does maintenance therapy afterward. Most patients will relapse and need continuous therapy to keep the disease controlled. Novel therapies (chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy, bispecific antibodies, antibody-drug conjugates and other inhibitors) are currently used for relapsed myeloma.

cards.t: Multiple myeloma prognosis and patient education
q: what is the prognosis of multiple myeloma
what should patients know about myeloma
how long do myeloma patients survive
cards.x:
Five-year relative survival for multiple myeloma is approximately 60% (2018 to 2022 data). Each line of therapy gives shorter remissions, and the disease remains incurable and fatal, although newer therapies may change that: recent studies suggest newly diagnosed patients today may survive more than 10 years.

For the patient this means treatment is likely lifelong, with periods of remission (disease control) followed by worsening symptoms, and life-long follow-up for lab monitoring and treatment. Care is by a hematologist/oncologist, ideally a myeloma expert.

cards.t: MGUS: monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance
q: what is MGUS
what are the criteria for MGUS
how often does MGUS become myeloma
cards.x:
Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) is a low-level clonal plasma cell disorder that is, by definition, asymptomatic. The criteria are an M-protein (monoclonal protein, the single overproduced antibody) under 3 g/dL, clonal bone marrow plasma cells under 10%, and no myeloma-defining characteristics.

The risk of progression to multiple myeloma is about 1% per year. It is a risk factor for myeloma rather than myeloma itself.

cards.t: Smoldering myeloma
q: what is smoldering myeloma
what are the criteria for smoldering myeloma
does smoldering myeloma need treatment
cards.x:
Smoldering myeloma is an intermediate-stage clonal plasma cell disorder. As taught, it requires both an M-protein (monoclonal protein) above 3 g/dL and 10 to 60% plasma cells in the bone marrow, with no myeloma-defining events such as anemia, bone lesions or renal failure. The current international definition uses either one, so references differ.

It typically does not require treatment, though early intervention may be considered for some subgroups. The rate of progression to myeloma is approximately 10% per year, but some high-risk groups have a greater than 50% risk of progression within 2 years.

cards.t: MGUS versus smoldering myeloma versus multiple myeloma
q: what is the difference between MGUS and smoldering myeloma
how do you tell smoldering myeloma from multiple myeloma
what is the progression rate of MGUS versus smoldering myeloma
cards.x:
The three plasma cell disorders are separated by the amount of M-protein (monoclonal protein), the bone marrow plasma cell percentage, and whether there is damage:
- Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS): M-protein under 3 g/dL, plasma cells under 10%, no CRAB (hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions); progresses about 1% per year.
- Smoldering myeloma: M-protein above 3 g/dL and 10 to 60% plasma cells (as taught; references differ on and versus or), no CRAB; progresses about 10% per year.
- Multiple myeloma: 10% or more plasma cells (or a biopsy-proven plasmacytoma) plus one or more CRAB features; relapses and is incurable.

Quick way to separate them: the first two have no damage (no CRAB), and what divides them is how much protein and how many plasma cells there are.

cards.t: Which lymphomas, leukemia and myeloma occur at which ages
q: what age does Hodgkin lymphoma occur
which lymphoma occurs in children
which of these cancers are seen in older adults
cards.x:
These blood cancers cluster by age:
- Children: Burkitt lymphoma, the endemic type in sub-Saharan Africa and New Guinea (tied to Epstein-Barr virus); long-term prognosis above 90% in children treated early.
- Teens and young adults: Hodgkin lymphoma has its first peak in adults in their 20s; sporadic Burkitt is almost always under 35.
- Adults: diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most common non-Hodgkin lymphoma; mantle cell lymphoma has a median age of 60 to 70.
- Older adults: chronic lymphocytic leukemia (median age 70), marginal zone lymphoma, multiple myeloma (most diagnosed over 65), and Hodgkin lymphoma's second peak over 60.

Older age also worsens outlook: age over 60 is a poor prognostic factor in non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and older Hodgkin patients have inferior results.
